item.title: Hip Lateral Glide With Active Flexion — MWM Trial
clinicalUse: A patient says bringing the knee toward the chest is uncomfortable and a squat feels restricted. You establish a safe, reproducible hip-flexion comparable sign.
Consider a selected belt-assisted hip lateral glide only when joint-related pain/mobility impairment is suspected and screening supports a manual trial.
Hip therapy should be integrated with activity modification, strengthening and movement training rather than sold as a joint 'reset'.
patientPosition: Supine on a stable treatment table with the pelvis supported and the hip in a comfortable starting position.
The patient must be able to actively flex the hip without severe pain; stop before a pinching end-range that worsens with the trial.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the treated hip with a stable stance and a suitable wide mobilization belt applied by an appropriately trained clinician.
Keep the belt line controlled, avoid slipping and ensure the clinician can release the load immediately.
stabilization: Support/stabilize the pelvis so excessive lumbar rotation or pelvic hiking does not substitute for hip flexion.
Do not press or anchor over the femoral triangle, groin vessels or other sensitive neurovascular structures.
contact: Use a broad mobilization belt or clinically trained hand contact near the proximal femoral/thigh region, positioned to give a lateral accessory glide without compressing the groin.
Check padding, skin comfort and belt security before loading.
forceDirection: Introduce a gentle lateral accessory glide to the proximal femoral region while the patient actively brings the hip toward comfortable flexion.
Fine-tune the line of the glide only if the task becomes clearly more comfortable; Mulligan's intended trial is pain-free/beneficial rather than forced through discomfort.
dosage: Begin with just a few controlled, pain-free repetitions (for example 3–6) and retest independently before further sets.
Do not prescribe a rigid repetition count when the comparable sign fails to improve or symptoms become worse.
steps: Record a comfortable active hip-flexion angle or relevant squat sign, including pain location and quality.
Screen trauma, fracture/stress-injury concern, unexplained groin pain, marked irritability and hip red flags.
Set the patient supine; position the wide belt for a lateral glide with pelvic stabilization, avoiding the femoral neurovascular region.
Apply a modest lateral glide and ask the patient to actively flex the hip within a pain-free improving range.
Adjust the belt direction or stop if symptoms do not improve; never overpower a painful pinching sensation.
Release the belt and immediately repeat hip flexion without assistance.
Connect any useful change with graded hip strength and movement practice.
reassess: Same independent active hip flexion or squat
Ability to complete the target daily task without the belt
mistakes: Pushing into a painful pinch because the belt feels strong.
Claiming a lateral glide corrected a proven femoral-head displacement.
Allowing the pelvis to rotate so hip movement gains are falsely measured.
safety: Avoid routine mobilization if fracture/stress fracture, recent dislocation, severe trauma, unstable joint or major neurological/vascular issues are suspected.
Do not compress femoral vessels/nerve with the belt or force symptomatic end-range flexion.
Refer for further evaluation when severe groin pain, night/rest pain or persistent unremitting symptoms suggest non-routine pathology.
item.visualCue: Controlled lateral proximal-femur glide + patient active hip flexion → independent hip-flexion retest.

story.title: The hip that won't negotiate with the squat
story.scene: A patient begins a squat and feels an uncomfortable pinch near the hip. Instead of searching for a 'misplaced femoral head', the therapist first observes how hip flexion behaves without assistance.
story.clinicalDecision: With a stable, properly placed belt applying a measured lateral proximal-femoral glide, the patient actively flexes the hip. The therapist checks for a comfortable, clearly improving sign. If the pinch persists, the belt is not given the final word.
story.retest: The belt comes off. The patient repeats the movement, then progresses to strength and movement training if useful. A short-term gain is not permission to claim permanent joint repositioning.
story.punchline: The squat has no interest in your belt brand. It only cares whether it feels better.
story.evidenceCaveat: The 2023 hip clinical practice guideline supports multimodal interventions and allows joint mobilization for suspected mobility impairments, but notes limited evidence for isolated manual-therapy effects.
